content: Shingles, also known as herpes zoster, is a painful and blistering skin rash caused by the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus responsible for chickenpox. Symptoms of Shingles: The initial symptom is typically one-sided pain, tingling, or burning. This pain can be severe and often precedes the appearance of any rash. Red patches develop on the skin, followed by small blisters. These blisters eventually break, forming small ulcers that dry out and form crusts. The crusts usually fall off within 2 to 3 weeks, and scarring is uncommon. The rash typically appears in a narrow band that extends from the spine around to the front of the abdomen or chest. It may also involve the face, eyes, mouth, or ears. Additional symptoms may include: Abdominal pain Chills Difficulty moving certain facial muscles Drooping eyelid (ptosis) Fever and chills General malaise Genital lesions Headache Hearing loss Joint pain Loss of eye movement Swollen lymph nodes Taste disturbances Vision problems If the facial nerve is affected, you may experience pain, muscle weakness, and a rash on different parts of the face. Causes of Shingles: After a person has chickenpox, the varicella-zoster virus remains dormant in certain nerves in the body. Shingles occurs when this virus reactivates years later. The exact reason for the virus's reactivation is unclear. Most individuals experience only one episode of shingles in their lifetime. Risk Factors: Shingles can occur at any age but is more likely in individuals: Over the age of 60 Who had chickenpox before the age of 1 With weakened immune systems due to medications or diseases If someone who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine comes into direct contact with the shingles rash, they may develop chickenpox, not shingles. Diagnosis: A doctor can diagnose shingles by examining the skin and reviewing the patient’s medical history. Tests are rarely needed but may include a skin sample to confirm the presence of the virus. Blood tests may show increased white blood cells and antibodies to the chickenpox virus but cannot definitively confirm shingles. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact your healthcare provider if you experience symptoms of shingles, especially if you have a weakened immune system or if symptoms persist or worsen. Shingles involving the eye requires emergency medical care, as it can lead to permanent blindness if untreated. Treatment Options: Antiviral medications, such as acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir, may be prescribed to combat the virus. These drugs reduce pain, complications, and the duration of the disease. They are most effective when started within 24 hours of the onset of pain or burning, ideally before blisters appear. Antiviral drugs are usually taken orally in higher doses than those used for herpes simplex or genital herpes. In some cases, intravenous (IV) administration may be necessary. Corticosteroids, such as prednisone, may be used to reduce swelling and the risk of prolonged pain, although they are not effective for all patients. Other medications may include: Antihistamines to alleviate itching (taken orally or applied to the skin) Pain relievers Zostrix cream (containing capsaicin) to reduce the risk of postherpetic neuralgia Cool, wet compresses can help relieve pain. Soothing baths and lotions, such as colloidal oatmeal baths, starch baths, or calamine lotion, may reduce itching and discomfort. Resting in bed until the fever subsides is recommended. The skin should be kept clean, and contaminated items should not be reused. Non-disposable items should be disinfected or boiled before reuse. Isolation may be necessary while lesions are oozing to prevent spreading the virus to individuals who have never had chickenpox, particularly pregnant women. Prognosis: Shingles typically resolves within 2 to 3 weeks and rarely recurs. However, if the virus affects motor nerves, temporary or permanent weakness or paralysis may occur. Pain in the affected area may persist for months or years, a condition known as postherpetic neuralgia. This is more common in individuals over 60 years old. Possible Complications: Postherpetic neuralgia, characterized by persistent pain in the area of the shingles rash, occurs due to nerve damage from the outbreak. Pain severity can range from mild to severe. Other complications may include: Recurrence of shingles Blindness (if the eye is affected) Deafness Infections, such as encephalitis or sepsis, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems Bacterial skin infections Ramsay Hunt syndrome, if facial nerves are involved Prevention: Avoid touching the rash and blisters of individuals with shingles or chickenpox if you have never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine. A herpes zoster vaccine is available and is different from the chickenpox vaccine. Older adults who receive the herpes zoster vaccine are less likely to experience complications from shingles. Adults over the age of 60 should receive the herpes zoster vaccine as part of routine medical care.
